hints: Notice the question tells you both molecules have the same number of electrons, so think about what that means for London dispersion forces.
Compare the symmetry and electronegativity in $\text{CH}_3\text{CH}_3$ and $\text{CH}_3\text{F}$ to decide which one is polar and which is non-polar.
Remember boiling point rises when there is an extra intermolecular force to overcome, so link the higher boiling point to the additional force present in the polar molecule.
walkthrough:
**Check what is the same**

Both molecules have 18 electrons. That means the London (induced dipole-dipole) forces should be very similar in strength.

So the difference in boiling point must come from a different type of intermolecular force.

**Check polarity of each molecule**

$\text{CH}_3\text{CH}_3$ is symmetrical and made only of C-C and C-H bonds with similar electronegativities. It is non-polar with no permanent dipole.

$\text{CH}_3\text{F}$ contains highly electronegative F bonded to C. The $\text{C-F}$ bond is very polar, so the whole molecule has a permanent dipole.

**Link intermolecular forces to boiling point**

Non-polar $\text{CH}_3\text{CH}_3$ has only London forces between molecules.

Polar $\text{CH}_3\text{F}$ has London forces plus permanent dipole-dipole forces. More energy is needed to separate the molecules, so its boiling point is higher at 194.7 K.

options.A: Incorrect. $M_r$ of $\text{CH}_3\text{F}$ is 34 and $M_r$ of $\text{CH}_3\text{CH}_3$ is 30, but the question stresses equal electrons to show London forces are similar. The small mass difference is not the main reason for the higher boiling point.
options.B: Correct. $\text{CH}_3\text{F}$ is polar due to the electronegative F atom and has permanent dipole-dipole forces in addition to London forces. $\text{CH}_3\text{CH}_3$ is non-polar and has only London forces, so less energy is needed to boil it.
options.C: Incorrect. The $\text{C-F}$ bond is indeed strong, but boiling does not break covalent bonds. It only overcomes intermolecular forces between molecules, so bond strength inside the molecule is irrelevant here.
options.D: Incorrect. Hydrogen bonding needs H directly attached to N, O or F. In $\text{CH}_3\text{F}$ the H atoms are attached to C, not to F, so no hydrogen bonding can occur between $\text{CH}_3\text{F}$ molecules. This is a common trap when students see F in the formula.
